title: The True King
opening: What does it mean to recognize God as our King? In Revelation, heaven is filled with worship, reverence, and the willing surrender of crowns. Yet in the Gospel, some accept their king, others fear him, and still others reject him entirely. Perhaps these readings reveal something about the many ways we respond to God, and the love that makes our response meaningful.
body:
Today's first reading from Revelation is extraordinary. John is invited through an open door into heaven, where he witnesses a vision of God's majesty. He sees a throne surrounded by brilliance resembling jasper and carnelian, an emerald-like rainbow, twenty-four elders seated on thrones wearing golden crowns, and something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal. There are flashes of lightning, sounds of thunder, and seven flaming torches before the throne. It is an overwhelming description, filled with imagery that seems almost impossible to comprehend.

And then there are the four living creatures, each with six wings and covered with eyes. One resembles a lion, another a calf, another has a human face, and the fourth resembles an eagle in flight. In Catholic tradition, these creatures have been associated with the four Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. They can also represent the fullness of creation: wild animals, domesticated animals, humanity, and birds. Their six wings recall the seraphim described by Isaiah, while their many eyes suggest watchfulness and awareness. John draws upon images found throughout Scripture to describe the heavenly worship surrounding God.

The creatures continually proclaim, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.” And whenever they give glory to God, the twenty-four elders fall before Him, lay down their crowns, and worship the One who created all things. The elders are often understood as representing the fullness of God's people, recalling the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles.

As I read this, I found myself wondering whether God really wants all this worship. I have never questioned that all glory belongs to Him, nor do I question the genuine love and reverence of those in His presence. But I know God as loving and humble, and I found myself imagining Him asking them to rise, appreciating their love without needing such continual expressions of honor.

Yet perhaps I was looking at the scene from the wrong perspective. God does not need our worship to become greater than He already is. The creatures and elders are not described as being commanded to bow. Their adoration appears to flow freely from their recognition of who God is.

And that is something I understand. When love is present in its fullness, all it can do is flow freely. Perhaps that is what John is witnessing. The elders are not surrendering their crowns because God needs their submission, but because they recognize that everything they possess comes from Him. Their worship is an expression of love, gratitude, and reverence. They are in the presence of their Creator, and their response is complete acceptance of Him.

Then we come to today's Gospel, and the contrast is remarkable.

Jesus tells the Parable of the Ten Gold Coins because the people believe the Kingdom of God is about to appear immediately. A nobleman leaves to receive kingship and entrusts ten servants with one gold coin each, instructing them to conduct business until he returns. Unlike the Parable of the Talents we reflected upon recently, where the servants received different amounts according to their abilities, here every servant begins with exactly the same amount.

But something interesting happens. Although ten servants receive coins, Jesus tells us what happened with only three. The first earns ten additional coins and is rewarded with authority over ten cities. The second earns five and receives authority over five cities. The third returns the original coin, explaining that he kept it hidden because he feared his master.

What happened to the other seven?

Scripture doesn't tell us. We cannot assume they failed, refused to return, or were still waiting. Yet I find myself wondering about those seven whose stories remain unknown. Could they remind us of the many people whose relationships with God are still unfolding, or perhaps those who have yet to respond to Him? I cannot say that this is what Jesus intended, but it is interesting that we are given only three accounts when ten servants were entrusted with the same gift.

Perhaps the three responses reveal something about the different ways we live our relationship with God. Some are fruitful, some accomplish less but remain faithful, and some allow fear to prevent them from acting. Yet there are many others whose stories we do not know. We cannot see the entirety of another person's relationship with God, nor can we know everything He may be doing within them.

But the Gospel introduces another group entirely: the citizens who reject the nobleman's kingship. They send a delegation declaring, “We do not want this man to be our king.” They are not merely afraid of him, as the third servant is. They openly reject his authority.

And the ending is troubling. The nobleman calls these people his enemies and orders them slain in his presence. It is a harsh conclusion, especially when we think of the loving God revealed through Jesus. The story may recall the political realities of rulers who sought authority and punished those who opposed them. We should not assume that every action of this human nobleman is intended to describe God's character. Nevertheless, Jesus does not remove the seriousness of rejecting kingship or the reality of judgment from His parable.

This is where the contrast between today's readings becomes especially meaningful to me. In Revelation, we see the complete and willing acceptance of God. The elders recognize His majesty and freely offer Him everything, even their crowns. In the Gospel, we see a very different picture: servants responding in different ways to what has been entrusted to them, and citizens who refuse to accept their king at all.

One reading reveals the fullness of worship in God's presence, while the other reminds us how complicated our response to Him can be during our earthly lives.

Perhaps the difference lies partly in how we recognize the One who rules over us. In heaven, the elders see God's glory and respond with love. In the Gospel, fear, responsibility, loyalty, and rejection all become part of the story. And Jesus tells this parable while His listeners are expecting the Kingdom to appear immediately, reminding them that there will be a time of waiting before its fulfillment.

I find myself returning to the seven servants whose stories remain untold. We know they received the same coin, but we do not know what they did with it. Perhaps that uncertainty reflects something about our own lives. We are all somewhere within our relationship with God, responding to what we have received, sometimes with confidence, sometimes with fear, and sometimes without fully understanding what is being asked of us.

I do not know how every story will end. That belongs to God. But I do know that what we have been given is meant to bear fruit, and that our response to Him matters.

And when I return to John's vision, I am reminded of something that changes how I see all that heavenly worship. God does not need to demand love. When we truly recognize His goodness, His majesty, and the source of everything we have received, perhaps love becomes the most natural response of all.

The elders lay down their crowns because they know whom they love. Perhaps that is the fullness of what we are all moving toward: not merely acknowledging God's authority, but coming to know Him so completely that our love flows freely toward Him.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  Your majesty is greater than anything I can imagine, yet You allow me to know You through Your love. Help me recognize that all I have comes from You, and teach me to receive Your gifts with gratitude and use them faithfully.  Lord Jesus, I know that our relationships with You are not always simple. We struggle with fear, uncertainty, and sometimes even resistance. Help me understand what You ask of me without allowing fear to determine my response. Give me the wisdom to recognize Your truth and the courage to live it.  I pray also for those whose stories I do not know, those still searching, those struggling to believe, and those who have turned away. You know each heart and every circumstance. May Your love continue to reach us in ways we may not yet understand.  And Lord, when I think of the elders laying their crowns before You, help me remember that true love does not need to be forced. May my love for You grow so freely and completely that gratitude, reverence, and faithfulness become a natural expression of all You have given me.
scripture: Revelation 4:1–11; Psalm 150:1–6; Luke 19:11–28; Ezekiel 1:4–14; Isaiah 6:1–3; Revelation 1:20.
theme: God's majesty, the freedom to love Him, and the different ways we respond to what He has entrusted to us.
